pages.title: Grouping, Proximity and Common Region
pages.content:
**The Laws of Proximity and Common Region** are often used in interface design.

It explains how people decide whether an **element** is a part of a group and are especially helpful for interface designers because they help set up a hierarchy by putting elements into groups.

Let's look at the application of each of these laws in web design!

pages.title: The ikea redesign
pages.content:
Check the two versions of Ikeas's product cart page.

Can you think of why the design on left was poor? 

In the old version of Ikea’s website, it was hard to tell where the quantity picker belonged. 

After redesign, the elements became not only well adjusted but also got a separating border between them. \
**The designers utilised the Proximity Law**.

pages.content:
That brings us to the definition of the law of proximity.

**"Elements that are close to each other are perceived to be related when compared with elements that are separate from each other."**

**The principle of common region says that items within a boundary are perceived as a group and assumed to share some common characteristic or functionality.**

The laws of Proximity and Common region are two of the 7 Gestalt Principles that guides interface designers to arrange elements on the interface to make it easier for users to make sense of the information.

pages.title: Padding and Margin
pages.content:
As we discuss the various aspects of spacing, let us explore the two key spacing terms. **Padding and Margins**

**Padding** is the spacing between elements and the related content inside it.
It determines how elements look and sit within a container. 

**Margin** is the space around an element. Margins are used to move an element up or down on a page as well as left or right.

pages.title: Typography
pages.content:
Perhaps no single topic is more underrated in website design than **typography**. 

Typography determines how text looks to the reader, how the words literally appear on a page or screen.\
On top of ease-of-reading, digital text must be designed for:
1. Shorter attention spans 
2. Skimmability
3. Accessibility
4. Multiple device types and screen sizes
